subtopics.title: MUnit HTTP and Database Mocking Examples
subtopics.meta_description: Worked MUnit examples showing how to mock an HTTP Request connector and a Database Select operation so tests run without any real network or database access.
subtopics.summary: Mocking HTTP and Database operations with mock-when and then-return lets MUnit tests exercise flow logic without ever touching a real network or database.
subtopics.content_html:
A flow that calls a third-party HTTP API and then persists the result to a database is exactly the kind of flow that is easy to leave untested, because testing it "for real" means depending on external systems being up, reachable, and in a known state. MUnit's mocking support removes that dependency entirely by intercepting specific processors and substituting a canned response.

Mocking an HTTP Request

Suppose a flow named get-customer-flow calls an HTTP Request connector to fetch customer data from an external service, then transforms the response. Instead of hitting the real endpoint, mock-when intercepts any processor matching the given criteria and substitutes a payload via then-return.

<munit:test name="get-customer-flow-returns-transformed-payload"
            description="Mocks the HTTP Request call and verifies transformation logic">

  <munit:behavior>
    <munit-tools:mock-when processor="http:request">
      <munit-tools:with-attributes>
        <munit-tools:with-attribute whereValue="Get_Customer_Config" attributeName="config-ref"/>
      </munit-tools:with-attributes>
      <munit-tools:then-return>
        <munit-tools:payload value="#[output application/json --- { id: 42, name: 'Ada Lovelace', status: 'ACTIVE' }]"/>
        <munit-tools:attributes value="#[{statusCode: 200}]"/>
      </munit-tools:then-return>
    </munit-tools:mock-when>
  </munit:behavior>

  <munit:execution>
    <flow-ref name="get-customer-flow"/>
  </munit:execution>

  <munit:validation>
    <munit-tools:assert-that expression="#[payload.name]" is="#[MunitTools::equalTo('Ada Lovelace')]"/>
    <munit-tools:assert-that expression="#[payload.status]" is="#[MunitTools::equalTo('ACTIVE')]"/>
  </munit:validation>

</munit:test>

Mocking a Database Select

Database mocking follows the same shape, matching on the db:select processor and returning a canned result set as a list of maps, which is exactly what the real connector would hand back to the flow.

<munit:test name="find-orders-by-customer-returns-order-list"
            description="Mocks the Database Select and validates row-to-payload mapping">

  <munit:behavior>
    <munit-tools:mock-when processor="db:select">
      <munit-tools:with-attributes>
        <munit-tools:with-attribute whereValue="Orders_DB_Config" attributeName="config-ref"/>
      </munit-tools:with-attributes>
      <munit-tools:then-return>
        <munit-tools:payload value="#[[
          { orderId: 1001, customerId: 42, total: 89.99 },
          { orderId: 1002, customerId: 42, total: 15.50 }
        ]]"/>
      </munit-tools:then-return>
    </munit-tools:mock-when>
  </munit:behavior>

  <munit:execution>
    <flow-ref name="find-orders-by-customer-flow"/>
  </munit:execution>

  <munit:validation>
    <munit-tools:assert-that expression="#[sizeOf(payload)]" is="#[MunitTools::equalTo(2)]"/>
    <munit-tools:assert-that expression="#[payload[0].total]" is="#[MunitTools::equalTo(89.99)]"/>
  </munit:validation>

</munit:test>

Matching Precisely with with-attributes

The with-attributes block is what keeps mocks from accidentally intercepting the wrong processor when a flow has more than one HTTP Request or Database connector configured. Matching on config-ref is the most reliable strategy since every connector configuration has a unique name, but you can also match on other processor attributes such as a specific query or path when a single config is reused for multiple operations.

Simulating Failures, Not Just Happy Paths

The real value of mocking shows up when testing error handling, since forcing a real downstream service to fail on demand is often impractical. then-return can be replaced with then-throw to simulate a connectivity error or timeout and verify the flow's error handler behaves correctly.

<munit-tools:mock-when processor="http:request">
  <munit-tools:with-attributes>
    <munit-tools:with-attribute whereValue="Get_Customer_Config" attributeName="config-ref"/>
  </munit-tools:with-attributes>
  <munit-tools:then-throw class="org.mule.extension.http.api.error.HttpTimeoutException"/>
</munit-tools:mock-when>

Confirming a Mock Was Actually Called

Returning a canned value only tells you what the flow does with a given input — it doesn't confirm the flow actually reached that processor, or reached it the expected number of times. verify-call closes that gap by asserting on invocation count after execution, which is especially useful for confirming that a retry policy called an HTTP Request connector three times, or that a conditional branch skipped a database write entirely under certain input conditions.

<munit:validation>
  <munit-tools:verify-call processor="http:request" times="1">
    <munit-tools:with-attributes>
      <munit-tools:with-attribute whereValue="Get_Customer_Config" attributeName="config-ref"/>
    </munit-tools:with-attributes>
  </munit-tools:verify-call>
  <munit-tools:verify-call processor="db:select" times="0"/>
</munit:validation>

Combining a payload assertion with a verify-call check gives a much stronger guarantee than either alone: the first confirms the flow produced the right output, and the second confirms it got there by actually exercising the code path the test intends to cover, rather than short-circuiting somewhere earlier through unrelated logic.

Keeping HTTP and Database Mocks Independent

When a single flow calls both an external HTTP service and a database, it's worth mocking both in the same test rather than only one, since real flow logic often depends on combining their results — for example, enriching a database record with data fetched from an HTTP call before persisting it back. Defining both mocks in the same munit:behavior block, each scoped tightly with with-attributes, keeps the two independent so a change to one mock's canned response doesn't have unintended effects on the other's matching logic.

  • mock-when intercepts a specific processor type; with-attributes narrows the match to a specific config or operation.
  • then-return supplies a canned payload and attributes, standing in for a real HTTP response or database result set.
  • Database mocks typically return a list of maps, mirroring the real db:select connector's output shape.
  • then-throw simulates connectivity failures and timeouts to test error-handling paths without a real outage.
  • verify-call confirms a mocked processor was actually invoked (and how many times), complementing payload assertions.
  • Precise matching on config-ref prevents mocks from silently intercepting the wrong connector in flows with multiple similar operations.

subtopics.title: Testing Batch Jobs and Schedulers with MUnit
subtopics.meta_description: How to test a Mule batch job's on-complete phase and a Scheduler-triggered flow in MUnit by invoking the underlying triggered logic flow directly instead.
subtopics.summary: Batch jobs and scheduled flows both run outside a normal request/response cycle, so MUnit tests them by invoking the triggered flow directly and mocking its steps.
subtopics.content_html:
Batch jobs and Scheduler-triggered flows share a common testing challenge: neither one is invoked by an inbound request, so there's no natural request/response boundary for a test to call. MUnit handles both the same way — by treating the batch job or the scheduled flow as just another flow that can be referenced directly, then mocking whatever it touches internally.

Testing a Batch Job's On-Complete Phase

A batch job typically has a Process phase that operates on individual records, and an On Complete phase that runs once after all records finish, often used to log summary statistics or send a notification. The On Complete phase receives a BatchJobResult containing counts of successful and failed records, which makes it a good candidate for isolated testing — you can construct that result directly rather than running an entire batch job through thousands of records.

<munit:test name="batch-job-on-complete-sends-summary-notification"
            description="Verifies the on-complete phase builds and sends a correct summary message">

  <munit:behavior>
    <munit-tools:mock-when processor="http:request">
      <munit-tools:with-attributes>
        <munit-tools:with-attribute whereValue="Notification_Service_Config" attributeName="config-ref"/>
      </munit-tools:with-attributes>
      <munit-tools:then-return>
        <munit-tools:attributes value="#[{statusCode: 200}]"/>
      </munit-tools:then-return>
    </munit-tools:mock-when>
  </munit:behavior>

  <munit:execution>
    <set-variable variableName="batchJobResult"
      value="#[{ successfulRecords: 97, failedRecords: 3, totalRecords: 100 }]"/>
    <flow-ref name="customer-import-batch-on-complete"/>
  </munit:execution>

  <munit:validation>
    <munit-tools:assert-that expression="#[payload.summary]"
      is="#[MunitTools::containsString('97 of 100')]"/>
    <munit-tools:verify-call processor="http:request" times="1">
      <munit-tools:with-attributes>
        <munit-tools:with-attribute whereValue="Notification_Service_Config" attributeName="config-ref"/>
      </munit-tools:with-attributes>
    </munit-tools:verify-call>
  </munit:validation>

</munit:test>

The key technique here is extracting the On Complete logic into its own referenceable flow (rather than leaving it as an inline, unnamed phase inside the batch job definition) so MUnit can invoke it directly and feed it a synthetic batchJobResult variable, instead of running the whole batch job with real input records.

Testing a Scheduler-Triggered Flow

A flow starting with a Scheduler component runs on a timer with no inbound message to send, which means a test cannot "call" it the way it would call an HTTP-triggered flow. The practical approach is to split the flow in two: a thin flow containing only the Scheduler source, and a second, referenceable flow containing the actual logic that the Scheduler triggers via flow-ref. MUnit then tests the second flow directly, bypassing the Scheduler component entirely, since the test doesn't want to actually wait for a timer to fire.

<munit:test name="nightly-cleanup-flow-removes-expired-records"
            description="Invokes the scheduler's target logic flow directly, without waiting on the timer">

  <munit:behavior>
    <munit-tools:mock-when processor="db:delete">
      <munit-tools:with-attributes>
        <munit-tools:with-attribute whereValue="Cleanup_DB_Config" attributeName="config-ref"/>
      </munit-tools:with-attributes>
      <munit-tools:then-return>
        <munit-tools:payload value="#[{ affectedRows: 12 }]"/>
      </munit-tools:then-return>
    </munit-tools:mock-when>
  </munit:behavior>

  <munit:execution>
    <flow-ref name="nightly-cleanup-logic"/>
  </munit:execution>

  <munit:validation>
    <munit-tools:assert-that expression="#[payload.affectedRows]" is="#[MunitTools::equalTo(12)]"/>
  </munit:validation>

</munit:test>

Why Splitting Trigger From Logic Matters

Both examples rely on the same architectural habit: keeping the trigger component (Scheduler, or the batch job's phase wiring) as thin as possible, and moving the actual business logic into a separately named, referenceable flow. This isn't just a testing convenience — it also makes the logic reusable if it ever needs to be triggered a different way, such as manually via an admin endpoint in addition to the nightly schedule.

  • Batch and Scheduler flows have no natural request to send, so tests invoke the underlying logic flow directly via flow-ref.
  • Splitting trigger components (Scheduler, batch phase wiring) from business logic into separate flows is what makes direct invocation possible.
  • For batch On Complete testing, construct a synthetic batchJobResult variable rather than running a full batch with real records.
  • verify-call confirms a mocked processor was actually invoked the expected number of times, not just that the flow didn't error.
  • This pattern keeps tests fast and deterministic by avoiding real timers and large record sets entirely.

subtopics.title: MUnit Best Practices and CI/CD Integration
subtopics.meta_description: Practical MUnit best practices and how to run munit:test with enforced coverage thresholds via the Mule Maven plugin inside a CI/CD pipeline reliably.
subtopics.summary: Running MUnit as an enforced, coverage-gated step in the Maven build turns tests from an optional habit into a build-breaking safety net.
subtopics.content_html:
Writing MUnit tests is only half the story — the other half is making sure they actually run on every change, and that a drop in coverage or a broken test fails the build loudly rather than getting merged quietly. This comes down to a handful of practices in how flows are structured, plus a small amount of Maven and pipeline configuration.

Design Flows to Be Testable

Flows that mix a trigger (HTTP Listener, Scheduler, batch phase) directly with business logic in the same flow are harder to test in isolation, because the trigger component itself can't be easily invoked from a test. Extracting the logic into its own named, referenceable flow — called via flow-ref from the trigger flow — means the test suite can invoke that logic flow directly, without needing to simulate an HTTP request or wait on a timer. This single habit is responsible for most of the difference between a codebase that's pleasant to test and one where every test needs elaborate workarounds.

Avoid Hardcoded Test Data

Hardcoded values scattered across dozens of test files make it hard to tell which value a given assertion actually depends on, and they make updating a shared test fixture painful. Centralizing common test payloads and mock responses in reusable DataWeave files under src/test/resources, referenced from multiple tests, keeps fixtures consistent and makes it obvious when a change to expected data is intentional versus accidental.

<munit-tools:then-return>
  <munit-tools:payload value="#[readUrl('classpath://testdata/customer-response.json', 'application/json')]"/>
</munit-tools:then-return>

Running MUnit via the Mule Maven Plugin

The munit-maven-plugin, driven through the Mule Maven Plugin, runs the full MUnit suite as part of the Maven build lifecycle, meaning mvn test (or mvn verify) executes every MUnit test in the project the same way a CI pipeline would, with no separate tooling required.

<plugin>
  <groupId>com.mulesoft.munit.tools</groupId>
  <artifactId>munit-maven-plugin</artifactId>
  <version>3.3.0</version>
  <executions>
    <execution>
      <id>test</id>
      <phase>test</phase>
      <goals>
        <goal>test</goal>
        <goal>coverage-report</goal>
      </goals>
    </execution>
  </executions>
  <configuration>
    <coverage>
      <runCoverage>true</runCoverage>
      <failBuild>true</failBuild>
      <requiredApplicationCoverage>80</requiredApplicationCoverage>
      <requiredResourceCoverage>70</requiredResourceCoverage>
    </coverage>
  </configuration>
</plugin>

With failBuild set to true, if application coverage drops below the configured threshold — say a new flow was added with no corresponding test — the Maven build fails, which in turn fails the pipeline. This is what turns coverage from an informational metric into an enforced gate.

Wiring It Into a CI/CD Pipeline

Because the tests run through a standard Maven phase, most CI/CD tools need nothing more than an ordinary build step.

mvn clean test \
  -Dmule.env=test \
  -DfailIfNoTests=false

Running this on every pull request, before merge, ensures a broken test or an insufficiently tested new flow is caught before it reaches a shared branch, rather than being discovered later during a deployment. Publishing the generated coverage report (typically Cobertura or a similar format) as a pipeline artifact also gives reviewers a quick way to see exactly which lines are untested, rather than trusting a single pass/fail percentage.

Other Practical Tips

  • Group related tests into suite files by feature area (e.g., orders-tests.xml, customers-tests.xml) rather than one enormous test file, so failures are easy to locate.
  • Use munit:before-test and munit:after-test blocks for setup/teardown shared across a suite instead of repeating it in every test.
  • Keep mock configuration close to the specific test that needs it rather than global, to avoid one test's mock silently affecting another.
  • Extracting business logic into referenceable flows, separate from triggers, is the single biggest enabler of testability.
  • Centralized test fixtures in src/test/resources reduce duplication and make intentional data changes easier to spot.
  • The munit-maven-plugin's coverage-report goal, combined with failBuild and threshold settings, turns coverage into a build gate.
  • Running mvn test in CI on every pull request catches undertested or broken flows before merge.
  • Publishing coverage reports as pipeline artifacts helps reviewers see exactly what's untested, not just a percentage.
